extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly; amateur and professional natural philosophers and general readers interested in hands-on physical experiments and popular scientific exposition
extracted.subtask_description: A popular-science magazine article that both describes natural phenomena (vortex rings) and gives practical, hands-on experimental procedures and observational guidance for reproducing and studying them. Also contains a separate essay compiling comparative biological/anthropological measures of sex differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of liquids for visible vortex formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Best to employ liquids differing but little from each other, or at least such as were easily diffusible in each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a variety of colored liquids and adjust density slightly (with alcohol, glycerine, or sugar) so the colored liquid is only a little less dense than the other; this reduces the action of gravity and allows ascending or descending currents to be obtained at will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optical arrangement for observing filiform osmotic currents
rubrics_metrics.description: By carefully taking advantage of the refracting and magnifying properties of cylindrical glasses, one may distinguish slight thin trains indicative of movement between two liquids separated by a permeable membrane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cylindrical vessels/glasses as magnifiers; observe against very dark or very light grounds to reveal the filaments. Adjust lighting and background to make faint threads visible; use colored drops to enhance contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus: communicating vessels / lamp-chimney with membrane
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple apparatus dependent on the principle of the siphon — raise the level of the colored liquid in the glass to change the rate of flow, or use a lamp-chimney corked at the bottom connected by a tube to a second vessel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a glass tube is not at hand, communicate via a bird's quill, thin straw, or a pinhole in membrane. Regulate flow with a string, nippers, or by inclosing an air bubble above the liquid and covering top with a membrane to vary pressure without changing liquid level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to produce a colored ring (drop expulsion procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring the orifice and the surface of separation of the two liquids to the same level and give a gentle push; a swelled fungus-like form with backward rotation issues and develops into a whirling scroll that forms the ring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver a gently tinted drop from about an inch height into a still colorless mass or use taps on a membrane to expel rings; follow the sequence illustrated (expansion, hollowing, folding back of edges, rolling up of spirals) to produce vortex rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulating density to retard descent and isolate phases
rubrics_metrics.description: With a little alcohol, or a trace of glycerine or sugar, one may modify insensibly the density of the liquids, reduce the action of gravity to a minimum, and have at will ascending or descending currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small adjustments in density to slow motion so different phases (e.g., swellings and attenuations) are more visible for study and photography/sketching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of perforated disk and membrane to generate repeatable rings
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the membrane as the bottom of the vessel and use a hole pierced in a disk forced into the middle of the tube; this instrument gives, at each expulsion of the colored ring, a corresponding return (negative) ring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the orifice/disk assembly in a lamp-chimney or tube; tapping the membrane produces successive rings; experiment with orifice size and shape to study paired positive/negative rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility enhancement using particulate tracers
rubrics_metrics.description: Myriads of little oily drops, an emulsion, superficial dust, or imperceptible grains of coloring substance put upon the surface render visible the annular constitution and descending trains of vortices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use emulsions (e.g., ginger emulsion), dust on a porcelain plate, ink, or sugar to trace flows; add tracer particles/dyes judiciously so as not to overly disturb the fluid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background and lighting for revealing internal structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A very light or a very dark ground, according to the character of the colored liquid, is required in order to discover the frame-work and the processes of the formation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose background contrast based on dye color; bright illumination from below or side-lighting can help reveal fine horizontal striae and the number/divergence of rollings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Producing large vapor/smoke rings and role of opening shape
rubrics_metrics.description: Vapors of certain chemicals in a box or a soap-bubble filled with smoke produce wreaths several inches in diameter; the shape of the opening has little influence upon the rings which are driven through a hole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a box (even made of playing-cards) with an opening and a slight blow to emit smoke rings; try square or rectangular holes and combinations of slits to create composite or vibrating rings (as described by Thomson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-ring interaction behaviors
rubrics_metrics.description: If two rings are sprung in succession they tend to overtake and cross each other alternately with damage if large; if they merely graze edges they change shape without breaking and then rebound to original form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study interactions in liquids for clearer behavior; fire rings from different boxes to observe mutual play and elastic rebound; note that grazing collisions may preserve vorticity and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elasticity and conservation of vorticity
rubrics_metrics.description: This power of annular elasticity is a striking characteristic: in a perfect fluid vortical movement can neither be created nor destroyed; the vortex-ring is indivisible and resists severing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect to 'cut' or permanently mar a vortex-ring; experiments should account for conservation of vorticity and energy exchanges with ambient friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity: household demonstrations and materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments within the reach of everyone: a penful of ink, a bit of sugar, a piece of thread, a soap-bubble bursting, or drawing spoon/knife over surface produce observable vortices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple items: a thread as capillary siphon for continuous movements, a spoon edge to create vertical half-rings, soap-bubbles with smoke, or boxes to blow rings — accessible demonstration recipe list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation of secondary nuclei and ring fragmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Most frequently denser nuclei appear in rings' interior, which descend as if suspended from elastic arches and may produce secondary rings that remain attached or separate into several smaller rings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for internal denser droplets/nuclei that can generate secondary rings; use slower descent (by density adjustment) to observe formation and detachment of secondary vortices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus variants: communicating vessels and siphon regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a system of communicating vessels (lamp-chimney, corked and connected by tube) or a simple capillary siphon (thread) may obviate manual difficulties and regulate flow rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement threaded control (string/nippers) or vary head by raising the colored liquid level; use a bubble and membrane to modify pressure without changing level for more precise control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for observing osmotic interchange threads
rubrics_metrics.description: When two liquids with strong affinity are brought into intimate contact across a permeable membrane they may take course across each other in distinct threads that present alternately swellings and attenuations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments to isolate drops and retard descent to visualize periodic swellings; observe from above for circular ring profiles or from the side for axial sections (see fig. 2 schematics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of smoke and phosphorescent fumes to create visible wreaths
rubrics_metrics.description: Smoke from tobacco, vapors of phosphoric acid or muriate of ammonia, or bubbles of phosphoretted hydrogen produce white wreaths and ring-clouds which can be ejected and studied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generate smoke within a chamber and expel through an aperture with a slight blow; use different gas/vapor sources for varying density and contrast; photographic capture recommended for fleeting forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Helmholtz spoon/knife surface-drawing method
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing the rounded end of a spoon or knife over the surface produces a vertical half-ring with internal contour matching the semicircular edge and related diametrical sections on surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this simple method for qualitative study of scrolls and mutual reactions of vortices (e.g., cream in coffee) and reproduce similar effects on a bath-tub scale for demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative-evolutionary framing of sex differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement that across the animal kingdom sexuality evolves: the female surpasses the male in many lower species, sexes become equal in intermediate species, and the male predominates in higher vertebrates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative examples (cephalopods, cirripeds, annelids, bees, fishes, birds, mammals) to frame hypotheses about human sex differences as part of a broader zoological pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nutritive and hematological metrics for sex comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Men have denser redder blood, more red globules and haemoglobin, fewer white globules, and less water; measurements by Quinquand, Korniloff, Malassez indicate quantitative differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare red-cell counts and hemoglobin concentration; consider caloric intake and observed differences in appetite/feeding frequency; note institutional/charitable data as supporting observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respiratory and metabolic measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Men exhibit stronger respiratory phenomena: larger pulmonary capacity (women ~1 pint less), men absorb more oxygen, exhale more carbonic acid, higher temperature, and differing pulse/respiration rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spirometry (pulmonary capacity), gas exchange measurements (O2 uptake, CO2 exhalation), and pulse/temperature records to quantify sex differences across ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeletal and bone composition criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative weight of the skeleton to total body weight is less in women; male bones richer in inorganic matter at age thirty (more carbonate of lime, less phosphate), per Milne-Edwards and Topinard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess bone mineral content, relative skeletal weight, and proportions (e.g., clavicle/humerus ratios) when comparing sexes or different races; account for age and stature normalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphometric body-size and voice pitch comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Male individuals are generally larger and heavier (average male-female height difference ~12 cm); female voice is consistently higher — cited as an octave higher than male.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect anthropometric data (height, weight, limb proportions) and acoustic measures (fundamental frequency) to document these differences; control for population/racial variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muscle strength and motor-precision metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Male muscular system is better developed and more vigorous; dynamometer measures show women's muscular force (25–30 yrs) about one-third less than men's. Men exhibit more precise movements (e.g., pianists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dynamometry for grip/force, motor-control tests for precision, and occupational performance measures (e.g., musicianship tasks) to evaluate relative motor capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cranial/brain volume and lobe development as intellectual proxies
rubrics_metrics.description: Male skull and brain are more voluminous/heavier (Broca, Parchappe, Huschke data), with frontal lobes (higher intellectual faculties) asserted to be less developed in women and occipital lobes (sentiments) more voluminous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify cranial/brain volume and relative lobe proportions using anatomical or imaging methods; interpret cautiously since morphological differences do not directly equate to cognitive capacity, and account for body-size scaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic and behavioral indices of morality and social roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Women commit a smaller proportion of crimes against persons, are more devout and charitable but possibly narrower or intolerant; differences attributed to shame, dependence, habits, and physical weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use crime statistics, religious participation, charitable activity rates, and sociological surveys to compare sexes; acknowledge confounding social/legal factors (laws made by men, social roles) when interpreting differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/intellectual participation as evidence of intellectual differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists of distinguished individuals in arts/science show far fewer women; women more engaged with novels while men prefer history, philosophy, and science; industrial employers report women as more assiduous but less intelligent for certain tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure representation across professions, award lists, publication records, and library borrowing patterns; consider historical access, education, and social constraints when assessing capability vs representation.
